# **ABSTRACT** {#abstract}

Home-based food businesses in the Philippines often rely on informal channels such as Facebook Messenger to receive and manage customer orders, an approach that becomes increasingly difficult to sustain as demand grows. To address this, Kitchen406 will be developed as an online ordering and product management platform that centralizes standard ordering, prepaid subscriptions, custom requests, checkout, and production-related workflows in one system. Customers will browse a self-service web storefront, purchase bread and pastry products, enroll in prepaid subscriptions, request customized cakes, manage delivery addresses, and pay through QR Ph. Owners and staff will use role-appropriate interfaces to manage orders, capacity, inventory, pricing, fulfillment, and sales analytics. Built through an agile, incremental approach, the platform will be evaluated through development testing and post-development user acceptance before deployment for live business use.

# **CHAPTER 1** {#chapter-1}

# **INTRODUCTION** {#introduction}

This chapter presents the background and primary motivation for developing the Kitchen406 platform. It outlines the statement of the problem, the specific objectives the project aims to achieve, the significance of the study to various stakeholders, and the scope and limitations to clearly define the boundaries of the proposed system.

## **1.1 Rationale** {#1.1-rationale}

Kitchen406 is a home-based bakery in Metro Cebu run by two owners, offering breads, pastries, and custom cakes on a made-to-order basis. Customers reach the business through social media and word-of-mouth, with most orders coming from repeat customers from the owners' immediate community. Orders are coordinated through Facebook Messenger and recorded on a whiteboard and a shared spreadsheet. This arrangement holds only because order volume is presently in a seasonal trough. Demand fluctuates sharply through the year, rising around holidays and occasions, where the same two-person operation has to manage volumes several times its usual output. This process is unsustainable at peak demand, when order volume is highest and the owners' available time is most constrained.

The business now plans to introduce a prepaid 4-week subscription line for bread and pastry products, which is produced in fixed batches and delivered on a scheduled day alongside existing custom and standard orders. The model originates with the owners rather than with customer demand, and its purpose is operational: batch production allows them to schedule activities, purchase ingredients against known quantities, and reduce the fuel cost of running the oven for scattered small orders. Each subscription creates a four-week fulfillment schedule that requires the owners to track fixed delivery days, remaining deliveries, and any skipped weeks pushed to the end of the cycle. With the owners' intended subscriber count goal, the business would need to track dozens of active subscriptions on overlapping and independently advancing schedules. A message-based intake channel can record orders but cannot automatically enforce production capacity limits or prevent overbooking across standard orders, prepaid subscriptions, and custom requests.

The same shift exposes gaps in the surrounding process. Batch production requires estimating ingredient needs from confirmed orders, yet no Bill of Materials (BoM) defines the ingredient quantities required for each product variant. Restocking is triggered only when supplies are visibly low rather than projected from a list of confirmed orders. Profitability is computed as total monthly sales against total monthly expenses, leaving per-product margins unknown in a market the owners describe as price-competitive. Additionally, the current process does not provide a structured way to record which owner prepared each product or determine their respective shares of the resulting sales and estimated profits. Payment is settled after delivery, an arrangement workable only because nearly every customer is personally known to the owners. The owners also intend to delegate order fulfillment and inventory tasks to hired assistance while limiting staff access to relevant operational information, a separation neither a spreadsheet nor a whiteboard can enforce.

Independent bakeries such as BreadHive demonstrate the use of prepaid subscription models in small-scale baking, where customers pay in advance for weekly bread shares collected on fixed days, with skipped weeks requiring prior arrangements (BreadHive, n.d.). Bakery inventory systems such as Cybake and Yokitup likewise illustrate how recipe costing, production planning, and demand forecasting help bakeries control material costs and reduce waste (Cybake, n.d.; Yokitup, n.d.).

In response to these needs, this study proposes Kitchen406: An Online Ordering and Product Management Platform, a centralized platform designed to improve order intake, production planning, and customer coordination for the bakery. The system will allow customers to place standard orders, enroll in prepaid subscriptions, submit custom requests, and track their order status, with all orders requiring payment in full online before they are confirmed. For the owners, the system will consolidate incoming orders into a single view, enforce capacity limits through an order calendar, monitor product availability and ingredient stock against confirmed orders, support pricing decisions through suggested selling prices based on estimated production costs and configurable markup, restrict staff access to order and inventory functions, and summarize business performance through a sales analytics dashboard. Through these capabilities, Kitchen406 aims to reduce the time spent manually handling orders, improve scheduling and inventory visibility, and provide a practical and scalable solution that supports the business as it grows toward daily operations.

## **1.2 Statement of the Problem** {#1.2-statement-of-the-problem}

### **1.2.1 General Objective** {#1.2.1-general-objective}

This study will aim to design and develop Kitchen406: An Online Ordering and Product Management Platform for a home-based bakery to support the bakery's business operations and customer transactions. 

### **1.2.2 Specific Objectives** {#1.2.2-specific-objectives}

Following the completion of this study, the following objectives are expected to be met:

1. Examine the existing ordering and customer communication processes of the bakery.

2. Design and develop an online ordering and product management platform.

3. Test and evaluate the platform for functionality throughout development, and for usability and user acceptance upon completion.

4. Deploy the developed platform to its production environment and turn it over to the owners of Kitchen406 for live business operation.

## **1.3 Significance of the Study** {#1.3-significance-of-the-study}

The output of the study will benefit the following:

**Kitchen406 Bakery**. It will replace a whiteboard and shared spreadsheet with a single production calendar covering standard orders, subscription fulfillments, and custom cakes, enforcing the owners' capacity limits at the point of booking rather than relying on recall. It will link confirmed orders to ingredient consumption so stock can be projected instead of inspected, and display estimated per-product production costs and profit margins to supplement the aggregate monthly calculations currently used by the owners. Above all, the system aims to support the planned prepaid subscription service by tracking commitments across overlapping four-week cycles. Managing these alongside seasonal order volumes would be difficult through the bakery's current manual process.

**Customers.** It will allow customers to browse the catalogue, place standard orders, enroll in prepaid subscriptions, and submit custom requests through a dedicated web platform, with order status updates.

**Home-Based Food Businesses**. It may serve as a reference implementation for single-kitchen operations considering a shift from chat-based order-taking to structured order and production management, demonstrating that fixed-term prepaid subscriptions and ingredient-linked costing can be adopted without the staffing, infrastructure, or capital of a larger food service operation.

**Researchers**. It will give the research team hands-on experience building a system from start to finish. They will work directly with a real client to gather project needs and turn basic business rules into strict system features. The team will also practice designing the system and connecting external software. Throughout this work, they will develop valuable skills in setting up digital payments and creating responsive websites.

**Future Researchers**. It will document the design of a fixed-term prepaid subscription system for a micro-scale food producer, an operating model distinct from the auto-renewing subscriptions common in commercial platforms.

## **1.4 Scope and Limitations** {#1.4-scope-and-limitations}

### **1.4.1 Scope of the Study** {#1.4.1-scope-of-the-study}

The primary scope of the study covers the development of the Kitchen406 platform. Specifically, the system includes the following components:

1. This study covers the analysis, design, development, and deployment of a bespoke web-based order management, inventory, and scheduling system specifically for Kitchen406, a home-based bakery in Metro Cebu. The system is tailored exclusively to the client’s operational workflows and is not designed as a general-purpose Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) product for other bakeries.

2. The customer-facing platform will support three distinct purchasing workflows: Standard Orders, Prepaid Subscriptions, and Custom Requests. Standard Orders cover one-time purchases of bread and pastry products available in the product catalog, Prepaid Subscriptions cover selected bread and pastry products offered through a four-week prepaid plan, and Custom Requests are limited exclusively to customized cakes. Customers placing standard orders may choose pickup or delivery as their fulfillment method. To prevent overbooking, the system will feature a capacity-control module that enforces daily product limits, strict cut-off times, and mandatory lead times for specific order types. These capacity baselines and cut-offs will be configurable by the administrators to accommodate fluctuating operational capabilities. The customer interface will also provide centralized tracking of order statuses to minimize the need for manual communication. All customer transactions require a registered account. Guest checkout is not supported. Customers must create and log in to an account before placing standard orders, enrolling in subscriptions, or submitting custom requests. Additionally, customers will be able to save, manage, and label multiple delivery addresses within their accounts and select a preferred address during checkout, with address details subject to final confirmation before order submission.

3. Products offered through the subscription program may also be purchased once through the standard ordering workflow; no product is exclusive to subscription enrollment. A one-time purchase of such a product is a standard-order item and may be combined with other products in the same cart. All items in a standard order share one selected fulfillment date. The system offers only dates on which every item can be fulfilled, including the configured production batch dates of any batch-produced product. If the cut-off or lead time for an upcoming batch has passed, the next eligible batch date is the earliest possible date for that product, provided the other items are also available then. Customers may choose between bakery pickup and courier delivery for standard orders. For pickup, customers will collect their orders directly from the bakery's location without incurring a delivery fee. For delivery, the system will apply the corresponding delivery fee, with orders delivered together incurring only one delivery fee. Standard orders use standard-order capacity regardless of the selected fulfillment method. Subscription enrollment remains a separate prepaid commitment consisting of four scheduled weekly fulfillments. Both workflows are subject to their respective capacity limits, lead times, cut-off times, blocked dates, and ingredient availability.

4. Customers may submit one review for each eligible purchased item after its associated standard order has been completed. For prepaid subscriptions, customers may submit only one review per enrollment, once all four scheduled fulfillments have been completed. Individual weekly subscription fulfillments are not separately reviewable. Each review may include a rating, an optional comment, and up to three photos. Admins have the authority to hide or unhide customer reviews and feedback in cases of malicious, spam, or inappropriate content.

5. For Custom Requests, the system will provide a modular cake configuration interface to generate a preliminary cost estimate. Customers may upload one to three reference images when submitting requests for customized cakes. Customers may specify their requested fulfillment date. This workflow will include an administrative review phase, allowing owners to negotiate final designs and issue a final quotation for customer acceptance. Once accepted and fully paid, the custom cake order will be confirmed.

6. For subscriptions, the system will allow customers to enroll in products offered through the subscription program through a prepaid plan consisting of four scheduled weekly fulfillments. Customers may select the available product variant, applicable subscription schedule, and delivery address. Customers may choose between courier delivery and bakery pickup for their subscription fulfillments. A delivery address is required only when courier delivery is selected. Since subscription payments are collected upfront, any applicable refund of prepaid delivery fees resulting from a change to bakery pickup shall be processed manually by the owners at the bakery, outside the platform. The system shall not automatically issue refunds or perform financial adjustments for such changes. The system will also manage predefined delivery cycles and allow one successful deferment per subscription, which the customer must submit before the affected fulfillment’s preparation day begins. 

7. The system shall check two replacement dates: the next day and one week after the subscription’s final scheduled fulfillment. It shall offer only dates with sufficient production capacity. If the customer confirms one offered date and the deferment allowance is unused, the system shall reschedule the affected fulfillment to the customer’s chosen date. If neither date has sufficient capacity, the request is late, or the allowance has already been used, the system shall reject the request, leave the original schedule unchanged, and not consume the allowance. A successful deferment may extend the calendar end date but shall not add a fulfillment. The system shall not search for a later replacement date.

8. The system will automatically calculate and reserve the required ingredient quantities based on confirmed orders using each product's Bill of Materials (BoM). Actual ingredient consumption will be recorded when production begins. It will alert administrators when stock falls to predefined thresholds and dynamically disable the ordering of affected products when required ingredients are fully depleted, working in tandem with the daily capacity slots to prevent overcommitment. Refund processing is outside the system's scope and will be handled independently by the owners.

9. The system will integrate PayMongo as its payment gateway, supporting QR Ph as its sole online payment method. To secure commitments, the system will enforce full online payment before confirming and scheduling production for standard orders, subscriptions, and finalized custom cake quotations. 

10. The system will include a sales analytics dashboard that distinguishes fulfilled product sales from recorded payments and displays sales trends, product performance, and available estimated production costs and profits. It will also support preparing-owner attribution for individual order items, allowing owners and authorized staff to record percentage allocations for standard orders, custom cakes, and individual subscription fulfillments, with the resulting owner-level sales and estimated profits reported to the owners.

11. The system will implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), allowing hired staff to access operational functions and information necessary for order fulfillment, production scheduling, and inventory management, including relevant customer contact and delivery details when required for fulfillment. Administrative functions involving financial reports, sales analytics, pricing configuration, and customer account management will remain restricted to the owners.

### **1.4.2 Limitations of the Study** {#1.4.2-limitations-of-the-study}

1. The subscription line is currently planned and is not yet operational, as it represents an entirely new offering for Kitchen406 rather than the digitization of an existing service. Consequently, the business has no historical subscription sales data to serve as a reference for evaluating demand and customer adoption. Therefore, actual subscription uptake and the accuracy of related projections cannot be assessed until the service is implemented and operational data becomes available.

2. Review moderation relies entirely on administrative oversight. The platform does not incorporate automated sentiment analysis, automated profanity filtering, or automated dispute-resolution mechanisms for addressing negative or malicious customer feedback.

3. Custom cake pricing is partially automated. The system generates a preliminary cost estimate based on predetermined cake options, such as size and other configurable components selected by the customer. However, this estimate is not the final selling price, as the system does not automatically determine additional charges associated with design complexity and customization requirements. These charges are evaluated and adjusted by the owners on a case-by-case basis during the quotation process. The owners issue the final quotation for the customer's review and acceptance before the order proceeds to full payment and confirmation.

4. The system does not support discounts, vouchers, or promotional codes. Order totals are calculated from product prices and applicable fees only, with no mechanism for applying price reductions, coupon codes, or promotional pricing at checkout.

5. Payment processing is limited to QR Ph through PayMongo, with no direct card payments, separate e-wallet integrations, or other payment gateways supported.

6. Delivery for standard orders and subscription deliveries is through a third-party courier, while custom cakes are delivered manually by the owners. Standard-order and subscription delivery are booked and tracked through the Lalamove API, with each week's subscription fulfillment represented as its own order for this purpose. Custom cake delivery logistics fall entirely outside the system, handled independently by the owners.

7. Subscription delivery addresses are fixed upon enrollment and cannot be changed after payment confirmation. This restriction maintains the prepaid delivery-fee arrangement and avoids additional payment or refund processing for address changes.

8. Costing accuracy depends on client-supplied data. Any figures the system produces around ingredient costing are only as accurate as the recipe and pricing data the owners themselves supply and keep current, since the system does not independently verify or update this information.

9. Sales analytics and owner allocations are limited to reporting purposes. Preparing-owner percentages are manually assigned and do not measure actual labor time. Estimated profits depend on the available production-cost data, while owner payouts, payroll, tax calculations, and full accounting reconciliation are outside the system's scope.

10. Inventory tracking is limited to a single-level Bill of Materials (BoM) structure that directly associates finished products with their required base ingredients. The system does not maintain intermediate or prepared components, such as dough or fillings, as separate inventory items with independent stock quantities or nested Bills of Materials. Packaging materials are included in product costing and may be recorded as inventory items, consistent with the system's inventory management features. However, the system does not provide dedicated functionality for automatically measuring production waste, ingredient loss, or actual batch yields. Such variations must be reflected through manually maintained ingredient quantities, inventory adjustments, or costing information provided by the owners. Consequently, the accuracy of inventory projections and product costing depends on the completeness and accuracy of the data entered into the system.

11. The study evaluates the system's capacity to handle orders, but cannot guarantee customer adoption. Whether end-users successfully transition from their current habit of informal messaging to utilizing the centralized web platform is a behavioral metric outside the control of this study.

12. The platform enforces minimum lead times across all purchasing workflows to ensure sufficient time for order preparation and fulfillment. Same-day fulfillment is not supported; customers must select a fulfillment date that satisfies the applicable lead-time requirements, cut-off times, and production availability.

13. The study does not include hardware integration. The proposed system is designed as a web-based solution and does not integrate with specialized hardware devices such as point-of-sale (POS) terminals, barcode scanners, weighing scales, or automated inventory-tracking equipment. Inventory updates and operational data rely on user input within the system rather than direct communication with physical devices.

14. The system's full operational capability relies on the stability of external services. Any downtime, rate-limiting, or service deprecation from these third-party providers is beyond the scope and control of the developers.

# **CHAPTER 2** {#chapter-2}

# **REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND SYSTEMS** {#review-of-related-literature-and-systems}

This chapter presents a review of existing literature and systems that are functionally relevant to the proposed system. Each system is examined with respect to its core capabilities, its relevance to the food and small business domain, and the specific functional limitations that justify the distinct features proposed in the Kitchen406 system.

## **2.1 Related Literature** {#2.1-related-literature}

### **2.1.1 E-commerce Adoption for Small Food Businesses** {#2.1.1-e-commerce-adoption-for-small-food-businesses}

Digital order intake and inventory tracking have both been shown to directly address the operational strain that manual processes place on small food businesses. In a case study of Nasi Cia, a small culinary startup whose manual order-taking process could not keep pace with rising order volume, researchers documented recurring operational problems: long customer queues, no centralized way to track incoming orders, and a costly dependence on third-party delivery platforms simply to manage order intake (Anugrah & Istiono, 2024). After the business adopted a purpose-built online ordering system, these operational issues were addressed directly, with 91.4% of surveyed users rating the resulting system favorably (Anugrah & Istiono, 2024).

A parallel strain is evident in the inventory management of small food operations. At Kava Coffee Shop, a small culinary business in Kudus, Indonesia, paper-based stock records led to inaccurate inventory counts, delayed restocking, and the absence of a mechanism for identifying depleting ingredients, increasing the risk of stockouts and overstocking of perishable raw materials (Taufiq et al., 2025). To address these challenges, a web-based inventory management system incorporating safety stock calculations, reorder point calculations, and minimum-stock alerts was developed and achieved a 100% functional test success rate. This result demonstrates that the tested system functions operated as intended, although it does not independently establish the accuracy of recorded inventory quantities against actual physical stock. Nevertheless, the study highlights the potential of automated inventory monitoring to support more systematic stock management and restocking decisions (Taufiq et al., 2025).

This reflects a problem structurally similar to Kitchen406's own situation: a home-based operation currently taking orders through informal, message-based channels, with no integrated system for tracking what has been ordered, by whom, or when it is due, and no mechanism linking those orders to the ingredient stock needed to fulfill them. This is a gap that a dedicated ordering and inventory platform is designed to close regardless of its downstream effect on sales.

### **2.1.2 Prepaid Subscription Models in Commerce** {#2.1.2-prepaid-subscription-models-in-commerce}

In a large-scale field experiment offering roughly two million newspaper readers either an auto-renewing or a non-auto-renewing promotional subscription and tracking them for two years, auto-renewing contract takers were about seven times more likely to continue into a paid subscription after the promotional period than those on non-auto-renewing contracts, reflecting strong consumer inertia around cancellation (Miller et al., 2023). However, the same study found that offering an auto-renewing contract measurably suppressed sign-ups in the first place, where 24% to 36% of potential subscribers avoided subscribing at all when the offer would auto-renew, apparently anticipating their own future. Over the full two-year period, the auto-renewing offer produced roughly 10% fewer total paying subscribers than the non-auto-renewing offer did (Miller et al., 2023). The study further noted that many of the subscribers retained through auto-renewal rarely used the service they were paying for, suggesting that short-term retention gained through a passive default can come at the cost of a smaller and less engaged subscriber base overall (Miller et al., 2023). For a fixed-term, non-auto-renewing model like Kitchen406's, this suggests that requiring customers to actively choose to re-enroll is a structure that plausibly works in the business's favor.

Prepaid subscription models in food commerce have been shown to reshape how consumers commit to and engage with a provider before goods are delivered. In a study of restaurant subscription platforms in Taiwan, prepayment-based subscription access to surplus food was found to depend on consumers' perceived usefulness and ease of use of the platform, with a more favorable attitude toward the subscription translating into a stronger intention to use it and, in turn, more favorable environmental purchasing behavior (Ma & Chang, 2024). This suggests that consumer willingness to commit to a food subscription in advance is closely tied to how clearly the platform communicates value and how little friction it introduces at the point of commitment, a consideration directly relevant to Kitchen406's own prepaid model: fixed-term, non-auto-renewing subscriptions.

This model specific to small food producers remain comparatively understudied, where the closest available reference is Community Supported Agriculture (CSA), where members pay upfront for a defined share of a farm's production over a set season, receive periodic deliveries for the duration of that term, and must actively choose to re-enroll once the term ends rather than being carried over automatically. A survey of those CSA subscription members found that renewal decisions and subscriber retention in a fixed-term model cannot be assumed and must be actively earned each cycle (Chen et al., 2019). While CSA operates on a seasonal, once-a-year renewal cycle rather than the four-week cycle Kitchen406 plans to use, the underlying structure, prepayment for a bounded term followed by an active, unprompted decision to return, is the same mechanism, and the comparative lack of literature on shorter, food-retail-specific cycles is itself a gap this study's documentation may help address.

### **2.1.3 Production Capacity Management Systems** {#2.1.3-production-capacity-management-systems}

Production capacity management becomes especially difficult for small and medium-sized bakeries because baking activities are constrained by shared, limited resources such as oven capacity and staff time, and a schedule that minimizes total production time does not automatically minimize idle resource time. In a study modeling three real production lines from small and medium-sized bakeries, a scheduling model built around the constraints most common in bakery settings found that the schedule with the shortest overall completion time was not always the schedule with the least oven idle time, meaning bakeries must actively balance these two goals rather than optimizing for speed alone (Babor et al., 2023). 

This reflects a broader principle established in the production scheduling literature. Because a business' capacity is finite, aligning it with incoming demand may require that some orders be turned away or scheduled deliberately rather than accepted as they arrive, since each order carries both revenue and a processing cost that must be weighed against the business's ability to fulfill it (Slotnick, 2011). Reviewing two decades of research on this order acceptance and scheduling problem, Slotnick (2011) frames the central decision facing capacity-constrained producers as twofold: which orders to accept, and how to schedule the orders that are accepted. Together, these findings support the case for Kitchen406's order calendar. Without a system that enforces defined capacity limits at the point of booking, a bakery managing overlapping subscription cycles and made-to-order requests may struggle to monitor its daily or weekly production capacity and prevent the acceptance of orders that exceed its available production limits.

### **2.1.4 Recipe-Based Inventory Management** {#2.1.4-recipe-based-inventory-management}

For small, home-based food businesses, recipe and ingredient costing is frequently handled through informal, memory-based methods rather than a structured system, which leaves businesses vulnerable to underpricing as ingredient costs shift. A qualitative case study of eight small-scale kakanin vendors in Pagadian City, Philippines, found that these home-based sellers computed direct ingredient costs primarily through habitual estimation and itemized manual calculation, shifting to more precise, written or app-assisted computation only when bulk orders, new products, or rising prices made errors too costly to risk (Antenero et al., 2026). The same study found that indirect costs such as gas, electricity, and packaging were typically absorbed into pricing through rough percentage-based allocations rather than exact costing, with vendors periodically adjusting their prices upward as overhead costs rose rather than recalculating costs systematically for each batch (Antenero et al., 2026). The authors concluded that these vendors would benefit from simple, standardized costing tools, such as recipe costing sheets or templates, to reduce their reliance on memory and estimation and to protect their margins more reliably. These findings reflect the current practices of Kitchen406, where profitability is assessed through total monthly sales and expenses rather than individual product margins, while ingredient inventory is monitored through manual inspection without a structured system for tracking recipe-based consumption.

### **2.1.5 Inventory Tracking for Bakeries** {#2.1.5-inventory-tracking-for-bakeries}

Inventory tracking remains a persistent operational challenge for small food manufacturing businesses, including bakeshops, many of which continue to rely on manual, non-automated stock management. A descriptive-comparative study of 200 food manufacturing SMEs in Davao del Sur, Philippines, drawn from five sub-sectors including bakeshops, examined four commonly used inventory strategies: Just-in-Time, ABC Analysis, Safety Stock, and Hybrid Inventory Systems (Adalim et al., 2025). While inventory managers across all four strategies reported generally satisfactory to very satisfactory perceptions of their effect on business performance, statistical analysis found no significant difference in actual business outcomes among the strategies, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on which strategy is adopted and more on how consistently and appropriately it is implemented (Adalim et al., 2025). The study further noted that bakeshops in the region often struggle to move past manual inventory handling, which limits their ability to adopt more advanced, technology-supported tracking methods common among larger firms. These findings suggest that for a small, two-person operation like Kitchen406, the specific inventory strategy chosen matters less than simply having a structured, consistently applied system in place, reinforcing the value of a platform that automatically projects ingredient consumption from confirmed orders rather than relying on visual inspection and ad hoc restocking.

Beyond the choice of inventory strategy, digitizing raw material tracking itself has been shown to directly reduce waste and improve cost control for small food and beverage businesses. In a case study of Cafe Rengganis, a small Indonesian food and beverage business that previously relied on manual recording for its raw materials, transactions, and financial reporting, the adoption of an integrated digital management information system reduced raw material wastage by 29.17 percent and shortened the time needed to prepare financial reports by up to 60 percent (Sari et al., 2024). The study attributed these gains to the system's ability to keep raw material records synchronized with actual usage in real time, which reduced the discrepancies between recorded and physical stock that had previously led to spoilage, overordering, and inaccurate cost figures under the manual process (Sari et al., 2024). This finding supports the design of Kitchen406's inventory module, which uses recipe-based ingredient quantities to project material requirements and reserve the necessary stock for confirmed orders. Actual ingredient consumption is recorded when preparation begins, allowing the system to distinguish planned requirements from physical stock deductions. By linking inventory records to production activities, the proposed platform aims to improve stock visibility, support timely restocking decisions, and reduce the risk of ingredient shortages. However, reductions in material waste and stockouts remain anticipated benefits rather than demonstrated outcomes of the proposed system.

### **2.1.6 Cost-Based Pricing with Approval System** {#2.1.6-cost-based-pricing-with-approval-system}

Cost-based pricing, in which a business calculates its production cost and adds a markup, remains a common approach among small and medium-sized enterprises because it is simple, transparent, and requires no specialized market research to apply, unlike value-based pricing, which depends on data the business often does not have the resources to collect (Stromeyer & Kurz, 2025). The same study cautions that more sophisticated, fully automated pricing models can become time and cost prohibitive for small businesses, since they demand data analytics capability and continuous adjustment that resource-constrained owners typically lack, and instead recommends simplified, modular pricing tools that reduce this burden without requiring the business to cede control of the decision (Stromeyer & Kurz, 2025). When participants were given the option to delegate pricing decisions to an algorithm, they were significantly more willing to adopt it when they could override its recommendations than when the algorithm's decisions were final, indicating a general preference for retaining final say even when a computational tool is available to assist the decision (Normann et al., 2025). 

Taken together, these findings support a pricing design in which the system calculates a suggested selling price based on the product's estimated production cost, including ingredient costs, packaging costs, and configurable utility overhead, together with an owner-defined markup percentage. The suggested selling price and estimated profit-margin information are presented to the owners for review rather than applied automatically. This approach supports cost-based pricing decisions while ensuring that the owners retain final authority over the selling price.

### **2.1.7 Upfront Digital Payments for Small Businesses** {#2.1.7-upfront-digital-payments-for-small-businesses}

Requiring payment at the point of order, rather than allowing payment on delivery or informal down payment arrangements, has been shown to directly reduce the rate at which customers cancel or abandon orders after placing them. In a study applying machine learning models to real e-commerce transaction data to identify the variables that best predict product returns, cash on delivery was found to be a significant driver of higher return and cancellation rates, since customers who have not yet paid retain little financial commitment to following through once an order has already been placed (Mishra & Dutta, 2024). Based on this finding, the authors recommended that businesses reduce their reliance on cash on delivery and instead incentivize upfront digital payment as a direct way to lower return and cancellation rates. For a small, home-based bakery like Kitchen406, where ingredients are often purchased or prepared specifically for a confirmed order, a cancelled or abandoned order after the fact represents a direct loss of ingredient cost and labor that cannot be recovered. Requiring digital payment upfront, rather than accepting cash on delivery or informal partial down payments as is common in the current message-based ordering process, gives the business the same protection this study identifies: it converts a customer's stated intent to purchase into a confirmed financial commitment before any resources are spent fulfilling the order. 

### **2.1.8 Analytics for Small Food Businesses** {#2.1.8-analytics-for-small-food-businesses}

Effective analytics for small food and beverage businesses depends less on the sophistication of the underlying model and more on identifying which data actually drives useful decisions. In a case study developing a sales forecasting system for an owner-operated food and beverage outlet, the most influential predictors of sales were found to be time-based patterns, specifically the hour of the day and the day of the week, followed by external factors such as promotional activity, holidays, or local events (Groene & Zakharov, 2024). The study further found that sales data broken down at this level of granularity allowed managers to move from relying on personal experience toward decisions grounded in the business's own historical patterns, directly supporting tasks such as anticipating demand peaks and planning production or staffing around them (Groene & Zakharov, 2024). This suggests that for Kitchen406's analytics dashboard, the most valuable reports are clear views of the business's own order history where sales broken down by day of week and time period, performance by product, and trends over time, can give the owners the same kind of pattern-level visibility that this study identified as the primary driver of better demand-related decisions for a comparably small, owner-operated food business.

While more sophisticated analytics platforms exist, research on how small businesses actually use data suggests that Kitchen406's dashboard should prioritize simplicity and direct usability over technical sophistication. In a qualitative study interviewing 50 small and medium-sized businesses in the United States about their business analytics practices, most reported relying on straightforward, low-cost tools rather than dedicated business intelligence platforms, citing limited budget and a lack of specialized data skills as the primary barriers to adopting more advanced systems (Kasiri et al., 2024). This reinforces that the value of an analytics dashboard for a business like Kitchen406 lies in making the business's own transaction data legible at a glance. This means surfacing figures the owners generate through daily operations, such as total sales volume and order quantity over a given period, sales broken down by individual product to identify which items are performing well, and trends across time periods such as day of week, echoing the granular, time-based sales patterns identified as most operationally useful in Groene and Zakharov's (2024) study of small food and beverage forecasting. A dashboard built around this kind of direct, order-derived reporting gives the owners visibility into their own sales history without requiring the technical investment that smaller businesses in the Kasiri et al. study consistently struggled to justify.

## **2.2 Related Systems** {#2.2-related-systems}

### **2.2.1 E-commerce Platforms with Subscription Models** {#2.2.1-e-commerce-platforms-with-subscription-models}

Subbly

Several commercial platforms already address recurring billing at scale, such as Subbly is a subscription-first e-commerce system that validates the core mechanics of online storefronts, automated payments, and customer self-service portals. Subbly successfully process prepaid commitments and provide a mechanism for customers to defer or skip upcoming deliveries. However, because Subbly is a general-purpose Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) product built to accommodate a wide public market, it inherently relies on standard inventory models rather than the ingredient-level tracking required by a micro-scale food producer. Rather than competing with Subbly's broad enterprise feature set, Kitchen406 addresses these specific operational gaps by acting as a bespoke, single-business solution, tailored exclusively to the unique workflows and strict capacity constraints of its owners.

BreadHive

While software platforms demonstrate the technical mechanics of recurring billing, existing small-scale bakeries provide the operational blueprint for prepaid food subscriptions. BreadHive, an independent bakery, successfully implements a “Bread Club” model where customers prepay for a weekly share of baked goods collected during a strict, fixed fulfillment window. Like the proposed Kitchen406 system, BreadHive secures commitments in advance and accommodates skipped weeks when scheduled beforehand, ensuring a predictable production schedule. However, BreadHive's publicly presented subscription offering does not establish whether its internal inventory processes include automated ingredient-level tracking. Kitchen406 addresses this operational requirement by integrating a Bill of Materials (BoM) that calculates ingredient requirements for confirmed orders, reserves the necessary quantities, and records actual consumption when production begins.

### **2.2.2 Bakery-Specific Inventory Platforms** {#2.2.2-bakery-specific-inventory-platforms}

Cybake

	Cybake is a UK-based bakery management software offering production planning, recipe management, and order processing. Supporting bakery operations from production planning through fulfillment is the primary focus of Cybake, a platform designed for retail and wholesale bakeries. The system links recipe information directly to production requirements, allowing ingredient consumption and procurement needs to be calculated from planned production quantities (Cybake Ltd., 2025). It also combines order processing, production management, inventory control, and delivery coordination within a single environment. A notable feature of the platform is its demand-driven planning approach, which can use sales data to forecast production requirements and adjust output accordingly (Cybake Ltd., 2025). This demonstrates how recipe, inventory, and production information can be integrated to support operational decision-making. However, Kitchen406 operates on a made-to-order model where production is driven by confirmed customer orders and subscription commitments rather than retail sales forecasts. Consequently, the proposed system emphasizes order-based production planning while applying similar bill-of-materials principles to project ingredient requirements and monitor stock levels.

Yokitup

Reducing the gap between incoming orders and production activities is a central objective of Yokitup. The platform presents confirmed orders in a production-oriented view, helping bakery owners determine what needs to be prepared without manually translating order records into baking schedules (Yokitup, 2026). It also supports recipe-based inventory management, stock monitoring, and cost analysis, allowing businesses to estimate ingredient requirements and track production costs (Yokitup, 2026). These capabilities illustrate how operational data can be connected to day-to-day bakery production. Unlike Yokitup, however, Kitchen406 is designed as a broader operational platform that combines online ordering, subscription management, capacity control, inventory monitoring, and business analytics within a single system. Rather than treating inventory and production as separate operational functions, the proposed platform links them directly to customer orders and recurring subscription commitments.

# 

# **CHAPTER 3** {#chapter-3}

#  **TECHNICAL BACKGROUND** {#technical-background}

	This chapter presents the concepts, technologies, and tools relevant to the development of the proposed system. The discussion focuses on the foundational technologies that support modern web-based business systems.

### **Frontend Technologies** {#frontend-technologies}

	Frontend technologies refer to the frameworks and tools used to create the user interface (UI) and user experience of a website or web application, which run directly on the client side within the user's browser (Kumar, 2025). In this system, the frontend will be built using Next.js, a full-stack framework based on React, which structures the user interface as a collection of reusable components rather than static pages. Through the App Router, Next.js distinguishes between Server Components and Client Components, allowing the system to decide where each part of the interface is rendered: server-side rendering (SSR) and static generation produce fully-formed pages that load quickly and are easier for search engines to index, while client-side rendering handles the dynamic, interactive elements that respond to user actions in real time. This hybrid rendering model ensures that pages achieve a fast initial load without sacrificing interactivity. Together, these technologies form the presentation layer of the application, translating raw data and business logic into an intuitive and responsive interface that end users can navigate with ease.

### **Backend Architecture**  {#backend-architecture}

	Backend architecture refers to the server-side structure of a web application, encompassing the logic, databases, and infrastructure that power its functionality behind the scenes (Gallardo, 2023). In this system, the backend is built within Next.js itself, which serves as a full-stack framework where the server-side logic resides in the same unified codebase as the frontend but remains architecturally distinct in responsibility. Rather than maintaining a separate server, the system uses Next.js Route Handlers and Server Actions to process incoming requests, execute business logic, and communicate with external services. Authentication and session management are handled through Auth.js, which verifies user identities and maintains authenticated sessions. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is enforced separately through server-side authorization checks implemented within the Next.js backend. These checks validate the authenticated user's assigned role before permitting access to protected operations and resources, ensuring that customers, staff, and administrators can only perform actions authorized for their respective roles. To bridge the application code and the database, the system employs Prisma as an object-relational mapper (ORM), allowing the backend to query and manipulate data through type-safe operations instead of raw SQL.

### **Relational Database Management** {#relational-database-management}

	A relational database management system (RDBMS) is a program used to create, update, and manage relational databases, which structure information into tables composed of rows and columns and establish links between data through common attributes (Google Cloud, 2024). In this system, PostgreSQL serves as the RDBMS, storing the application's structured data—such as users, products, components, orders, and transactions—in interrelated tables. Each table holds records as rows and attributes as columns, and relationships between tables are enforced through primary keys, which uniquely identify each record, and foreign keys, which reference records in other tables to link related data. This relational structure allows the system to model naturally connected information, such as associating an order with its customer and its constituent products, while normalization reduces data redundancy and preserves consistency across the database. To interact with PostgreSQL, the system uses Prisma as an object-relational mapper (ORM), which translates the application's object-oriented code into SQL operations, enabling the backend to perform type-safe queries without writing raw SQL directly. The database itself is hosted and managed on Railway, which provides the infrastructure for deployment, scaling, and maintenance.

### **Bill of Materials (BoM) Structure**  {#bill-of-materials-(bom)-structure}

	A Bill of Materials (BoM) is a comprehensive list of the raw materials, components, and quantities required to manufacture a finished product, serving as the central record that links a product to everything consumed in producing it (Heinz, 2025). In the context of Kitchen406, the BoM takes the form of a recipe structure, where each product in the catalogue—such as a specific bread or pastry—is linked to the set of raw ingredients it requires and the exact quantity of each. This structure is modeled in the PostgreSQL database through a join table that connects the product table to the ingredient table, with each entry recording an ingredient and the quantity that product consumes, allowing a single product to reference many ingredients and a single ingredient to appear across many products. Because the bakery produces goods from raw materials rather than nested sub-assemblies, the BoM remains effectively single-level, mapping finished products directly to their constituent ingredients without intermediate components. This recipe-driven structure supports inventory management and product costing. When an order is confirmed, the system uses the BoM to calculate and reserve the required ingredients. Actual consumption is recorded when preparation begins, while the same recipe quantities support product costing. In this way, the BoM connects the ordering, inventory, and pricing components into a single coherent chain grounded in each product's defined recipe.

### **Cost-Based Pricing** {#cost-based-pricing}

Cost-based pricing is a pricing strategy in which the selling price of a product is determined by first calculating the total cost of producing it and then adding a fixed markup percentage to arrive at the final price (Wall Street Prep, n.d.). In Kitchen406, this strategy is applied by computing each product's cost from the bottom up and then suggesting a price to guide the owners' pricing decisions. The system begins with the product's Bill of Materials, aggregating the cost of every raw ingredient in the recipe along with its packaging, which is treated as a direct material line rather than a separate expense. To this material cost, the system adds a per-product utility overhead value representing the gas and electricity attributable to the product; because true overhead cannot be calculated without reliable production-volume data, this value is not derived by the system but supplied by the owners, who set a general default that can be overridden for individual products whose baking demands differ, such as cakes that occupy the oven far longer than smaller items. The sum of ingredient costs, packaging, and utility overhead represents the product's total estimated production cost. The system calculates the suggested selling price by applying the administrator-configured markup percentage to this cost. It also calculates the estimated profit margin by subtracting the total estimated production cost from the selling price, dividing the result by the selling price, and multiplying by 100 to express it as a percentage. When the owners adjust the suggested selling price, the estimated profit margin is recalculated using the finalized price. This allows the owners to evaluate the profitability of each product before confirming its selling price. Since the calculation relies on ingredient costs and utility overhead estimates supplied by the owners, the resulting margin is an estimate rather than a measure of actual net profit. The system therefore serves as a pricing decision-support tool while leaving final pricing authority with the owners.

### **Capacity-Constrained Scheduling Logic**  {#capacity-constrained-scheduling-logic}

Capacity-constrained scheduling refers to allocating incoming orders against limited production resources, allowing businesses to determine which orders can be accepted and scheduled based on their available capacity (Slotnick, 2011). In Kitchen406, capacity-constrained scheduling is implemented through configurable limits enforced when customers book their orders. Capacity allocations are assigned according to the customer's selected fulfillment date rather than the date on which the order is placed or prepared. This approach allows the system to regulate the number of orders and product quantities committed for fulfillment within a given period. Although preparation activities may occur before the scheduled fulfillment date, these activities are reflected in the production schedule to assist staff in planning and organizing their workload. Consequently, fulfillment-based capacity limits regulate order acceptance, while the production schedule provides visibility into the preparation activities required to meet confirmed commitments.

### **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** {#role-based-access-control-(rbac)}

Role-based access control (RBAC) is a method of restricting access to system functions and information based on the permissions assigned to each user role (National Institute of Standards and Technology \[NIST\], n.d.). In the proposed system, RBAC applies to customers, staff members, and administrators, with different levels of access according to their responsibilities. Guests may browse publicly available products and bakery information without registering. Placing any type of order requires a registered customer account. Authentication allows the system to associate transactions, payments, delivery information, and subscription records with the appropriate customer while restricting customers to their own private information. For bakery operations, staff members are granted access to the information and functions necessary for order preparation, inventory management, production scheduling, and fulfillment. Staff members may record and update preparing-owner allocations through authorized operational interfaces but cannot access financial reports, sales analytics, product pricing configuration, or customer account management. These administrative functions remain exclusive to the Admin/Owner. By enforcing these restrictions through server-side authorization, the platform allows the owners to delegate operational responsibilities while maintaining control over sensitive business information and administrative activities.

### **Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)** {#application-programming-interfaces-(apis)}

An application programming interface, or API, is a set way for one computer program to ask another program for information or to perform an action (IBM, n.d.). It works like a waiter taking an order to the kitchen and bringing the food back. The system asks another company's system for something, and that system sends a response back. In the proposed system, APIs are used to connect the platform to outside services rather than building that functionality from scratch: PayMongo for processing payments, Lalamove for delivery quotations and tracking, Brevo and Semaphore for sending notifications, and Google Maps for location-based features.

### **Payment Gateway Integration** {#payment-gateway-integration}

A payment gateway is an online service that securely handles a payment between a customer and a business, checking that the payment goes through before the order is treated as confirmed (Zuora, n.d.). Simply, it is the middleman that takes the customer's payment and tells the business, "this has been paid." In the proposed system, this role is filled by PayMongo, a Philippine payment gateway that lets businesses accept payments through cards and e-wallets via a single API rather than dealing with individual banks directly (PayMongo, n.d.). One of the payment methods PayMongo supports is QR Ph, the national standard QR-based payment system set up by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas so that payments can move between different banks and e-wallets using one common type of QR code (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, n.d.). 

No order is confirmed until full payment is verified through PayMongo. This applies to standard orders, subscriptions, and finalized custom cake quotations. During checkout, a QR Ph payment session remains valid for 30 minutes, while the corresponding checkout hold reserves capacity and ingredients for 32 minutes, allowing two additional minutes for payment confirmation. Once payment is verified, the order is confirmed and its reservations are retained. If payment remains unconfirmed after 32 minutes, the system checks its status with PayMongo. Successful payments are confirmed, while failed, expired, or unresolved payments result in order cancellation and release of reservations. Unresolved payment records are retained for reconciliation. If payment is later verified as successful after the reservations have been released, the system rechecks the transaction’s applicable ingredient requirements, production capacity, blocked dates, and scheduling constraints using the original fulfillment details. If all requirements remain satisfied and the necessary resources are successfully reserved again, the system confirms the order. Otherwise, the order remains cancelled, and the customer is notified that the payment is eligible for a refund handled outside the platform.

### **Google Maps Platform** {#google-maps-platform}

	It provides a collection of APIs that let a developer show maps, look up places, and calculate routes. Three of these are used in the system: the Maps JavaScript API, which is used to build and display an interactive map directly on a web page and lets locations be shown, along with custom markers and interactive data layers; the Places API, which provides place details, search, and autocomplete for looking up and validating specific addresses or establishments; and the Routes API, which is used to calculate distance between two locations. In the proposed system, these services support the delivery side of the platform by allowing customers to search for, validate, and save delivery addresses through an autocomplete field, assign labels to saved addresses, and designate a default delivery address within their account. Customers can also select a saved address during checkout and visually confirm it on an interactive map before submitting an order. The Routes API is used to calculate the route and distance between the bakery and the selected delivery address to verify that it falls within the bakery’s serviceable area. This works alongside the Lalamove integration, which handles the actual booking and tracking of deliveries, while Google Maps Platform manages the location, address validation, and distance verification processes.

### **Notification Systems** {#notification-systems}

Sending customers timely updates is handled through two outside notification services rather than being built directly into the system. Brevo is a platform that provides an API for sending transactional and marketing emails, along with SMS and other messaging channels, used by businesses to handle their outgoing customer communications. Semaphore is a Philippine SMS gateway API that lets a business send text messages to mobile numbers on all major local networks, including Smart, Globe, and Sun (AgentiaSystems, n.d.). In the proposed system, Brevo is used to send email notifications, such as order confirmations or subscription reminders, while Semaphore is used to send SMS text messages, which is useful for customers who may not check email as often as their phone. These services are triggered automatically at key points, such as when an order is confirmed, when a delivery status changes, or when a subscription delivery is coming up, so the owners do not have to manually message every customer with the same routine updates the way they currently do through Facebook Messenger.

### **Logistics Provider API** {#logistics-provider-api}

A logistics provider API is a service that lets an application request delivery-related actions, such as price quotes and order tracking, directly from a courier company's system (Lalamove, n.d.). A logistics provider API allows applications to request delivery quotations, create bookings, and track delivery statuses through an external courier service (Lalamove, n.d.). In Kitchen406, the Lalamove API supports standard orders and weekly subscription fulfillments. During checkout, the system retrieves delivery quotations and includes the applicable fees before payment. Each subscription fulfillment is represented as a separate order for courier booking and tracking. Once an order is ready for delivery, the Admin/Owner manually initiates the Lalamove booking using its stored delivery information. The system then receives delivery-status updates through webhooks, allowing customers to track their deliveries without displaying the rider's live location. Custom cake deliveries are excluded from this integration, as they are handled directly by the owners. 

### **Hosting Infrastructure** {#hosting-infrastructure}

Hosting infrastructure refers to the servers and online platforms that make an application available on the internet so that users can access it through a web browser (Vercel, n.d.). The proposed system runs across two hosting platforms, each handling the part of the system it is best suited for. The main application, built as a full-stack Next.js project that covers both the customer-facing website and the business logic behind it, is hosted on Vercel, a platform designed for delivering fast, publicly accessible web applications (Vercel, n.d.). The system's data, including products, orders, and customer details, is stored in a PostgreSQL database hosted on Railway, a cloud platform that runs the database and other supporting background processes (Railway, n.d.). The application communicates with this database through Prisma, a tool that lets the system read and write data in an organized and consistent way (Prisma, n.d.). Separating the public application from the database in this manner keeps the running website and the stored data independently managed, which makes the overall system easier to maintain and update. 

### **Authentication & Session Management** {#authentication-&-session-management}

Authentication is the process of confirming that users are who they claim to be, typically by having them prove their identity with credentials such as an email and password, while session management is what keeps a user recognized as logged in as they move through the application (Auth.js, n.d.). In the proposed system, authentication is handled using Auth.js, a library built for Next.js applications that manages user registration, login, and session handling in one place. When a customer registers, they must confirm their account through an email verification step before it becomes active, which helps ensure that accounts are tied to real, reachable email addresses. Passwords are never stored as plain text. They are converted into a hash so that the actual password is never kept on file. Once a user successfully logs in, the system keeps them recognized as logged in across their visit and attaches the user's assigned role, whether customer, owner, or staff, so that the system knows not only who the user is but what they are permitted to access, which supports the role-based restrictions applied elsewhere in the system. 

### **Asynchronous Task Processing** {#asynchronous-task-processing}

Asynchronous task processing refers to work that a system carries out automatically in the background, either on a set schedule or in response to certain events, without requiring direct user interaction (Railway, n.d.). One common approach is a cron job, which executes tasks at predefined times or intervals without requiring someone to manually initiate them. In Kitchen406, background processing supports scheduled subscription reminders and the retrying of failed notifications. This allows recurring processes to run consistently without requiring manual intervention from the owners.

### **File Image Storage** {#file-image-storage}

File image storage refers to the use of a dedicated cloud service to hold and deliver a system's image files, rather than keeping those files on the system's own server or database (Cloudinary, n.d.). In the proposed system, Cloudinary stores product photos, up to three reference images per custom request, and up to three images per customer review. In each case, the image first passes through the system's backend, which then sends it to Cloudinary for storage. Rather than keeping the image files themselves, the system's database only stores the link pointing to each image in Cloudinary, which is retrieved whenever the image needs to be displayed. Handling images this way keeps the database lightweight and focused on the system's core data, while the storage and delivery of the actual image files are managed by a service built specifically for that purpose.
